# Lexicographic PLS-complete problems: Max-_k_-SAT, Abelian Permutation Orbit Minimization, and approximate pure Nash equilibria **Dominik Scheder**
TU Chemnitz, Germany **Johannes Tantow**
TU Chemnitz, Germany **Abstract** How hard is it to find a local optimum? If we are given a graph and want to find a locally maximal cut-meaning that the number of edges in the cut cannot be improved by moving a single vertex from one side to the other-then just iterating improving steps finds a local maximum since the size of the cut can increase at most |_E_| times. If, on the other hand, the edges are weighted, this problem becomes hard for the class PLS (Polynomial Local Search) [19]. We are interested in optimization problems with _lexicographic costs_. For Max-Cut this would mean that the edges _e_1_,...,em_ have costs _c(ei_)=2_i_. For such a cost function, it is easy to see that finding a _global_ Max-Cut is easy. In contrast, we show that it is PLS-complete to find an assignment for a 4-CNF formula that is locally maximal (when the clauses have lexicographic weights); and also for a 3-CNF when we relax the notion of "local" by allowing to switch two variables at a time. This result is interesting for two different reasons. Firstly, it offers another starting point for reductions to problems that are lexicographic by definition. We use these results to answer a question in Scheder and Tantow [20], who showed that finding a lexicographic local minimum of a string \(s\in\{0,1\}^n\) under the action of a list of given permutations \(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_k\in S_n\) is PLS-complete. They ask whether the problem stays PLS-complete when the \(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_k\) commute, i.e., generate an Abelian subgroup _G_ of _Sn_. We show that it does, and in fact stays PLS-complete even (1) when every element in _G_ has order two and also (2) when _G_ is cyclic, i.e., all \(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_k\) are powers of a single permutation \(\pi\). Secondly, we use it to further investigate the complexity of computing pure \(\alpha\)-Nash equilibria in congestion games. Using lexicographic 4-SAT, we obtain a simple proof of the PLS-completeness originally shown by Skopalik and Vöcking[21]. The simple structure allows us to also show hardness for exponential and polynomial delay functions with positive coefficients. Additionally, every resource is used by a constant amount of players and every player has a constant number of strategies. However, the degree of the polynomials is not bounded by a constant but grows linearly with the number of clauses and logarithmically with the approximation ratio \(\alpha\). **2012 ACM Subject Classification** Theory of computation \(\rightarrow\) Problems, reductions and completeness; Theory of computation \(\rightarrow\) Exact and approximate computation of equilibria **Keywords and phrases** PLS, local search, total search problems, permutations, congestion games \(\includegraphics{}\)

## 1 Introduction

Polynomial Local Search (PLS) is the complexity class of problems that require us to find a local optimum. Formally, a PLS problem is defined by a set I of instances, a set S of solutions, a function Feasible \(:\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\{\text{\texttt{true}},\text{\texttt{false}}\}\) telling us whether _s_ is at all a feasible solution to instance _x_, and a function StartSolution \(:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}\) where StartSolution(_x_) is always a feasible solution for _s_; further, functions Value \(:\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}\), where Value(_x,v_) computes how good the solution _v_ is for the instance _x_; and a _successor function_ Succs \(:\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}^*\), where Succs(_x,v_)=(_w_<sub>1</sub>_,...,w<sub>k</sub>_) means that _w_<sub>1</sub>_,...,w<sub>k</sub>_ are the neighboring solutions to solution _v_. We require that all feasible solutions to _x_ have the same length, and that all functions are polynomially computable. In particular, this means that each solution _v_ has at most polynomially many successors _w<sub>i</sub>_. A feasible solution _v_ is _locally optimal_ if none of its successors _w<sub>i</sub>_ is _better_, i.e., \(\text{Value}(x,v)\ge max_i\text{Value}(x,w_i)\) (for maximization problems) or \(\text{Value}(x,v)\le min_i\text{Value}(x,w_i)\) (for minimization problems). The goal is to find a locally optimal feasible solution.

The study of this class was initiated by Johnson, Papadimitriou and Yannakakis in [13]. In their work they showed that Flip is PLS-complete:

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Search Problem 1** (Flip)**.** _Given a circuit C with n input and m output bits; find an input_ \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) _such that_ \(C(x)\unknown_\text{lex}C(x\oplus\text{\texttt{e}}_i)\) _for all i_=1_,...,n. Here,_ \(\unknown_\text{lex}\) _is the lexicographical order on_ {0,1}_<sup>m</sup>, i.e., we interpret the outputs as binary numbers and compare them accordingly._

The instances of Flip are circuits; feasible solutions are bit vectors of the appropriate length; the function Value is given by the output of the circuit and the neighborhood of a bit vector are all bit vectors with a Hamming distance of 1.

In the realm of search problems, the notion of a _reduction from A to B_ requires a function _f_ mapping _A_-instances to _B_-instances and a function _g_ mapping _B_-solutions to _A_-solutions. Several search problems are known to be PLS-complete under these reductions:

**1.** LocalMax-_k_-SAT for \(k\ge 2\). Given a _k_-CNF formula \(F=C_0\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{m-1}\) with _n_ variables and clause weights _w_<sub>1</sub>_,...,w<sub>m</sub>_, find an assignment \(\alpha\) such that the weight of satisfied clauses cannot be improved by flipping a single variable (Krentel [16], Schäffer and Yannakakis [19]).

**2.** LocalMaxCut. Given a graph _G_=(_V,E_) and edge weights \(w:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\), find a cut \(V=S\unknown T\) such that its weight (the sum of weights of all edges crossing the cut) cannot be improved by moving a vertex from one side to the other (Schäffer and Yannakakis [19]).

**3.** Permutation Orbit Local Minimum (Polm): Given a string \(s\in\{0,1\}^n\) and permutations \(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_k\in S_n\), find \(\pi\in\langle\pi_1,\dots,\pi_k\rangle\) such that \(s\circ\pi\) is lexicographically locally minimal, i.e, \(s\circ\pi\unknown_\text{lex}s\circ\pi\circ\pi_i\) for all \(1\le i\le k\) (Scheder and Tantow [20]).

**4.** Finding pure Nash equilibria in congestion games, described in more detail in Section 2 below (Fabrikant, Papadimitriou and Talwar [7], Ackermann, Röglin and Vöcking[1]).

The first two are obviously in PLS. Polm is because membership \(\pi\in\langle\pi_1,\dots,\pi_k\rangle\) can be decided efficiently (Furst, Hopcroft and Luks [9]). For congestion games, the existence of pure Nash equilibria can be shown using an appropriate potential function that decreases whenever a player decreases their cost by changing their strategy (Rosenthal [18]), which then also shows membership in PLS.

As described by Giannakopoulos, Grosz, and Melisourgos [10], the function Value can be described as a function mapping a solution _s_ to some solution vector \(s'\) and the result is then

\(c\cdot s'\) for some cost vector _c_. In LocalMax-_k_-SAT, \(s'\) in position _i_ has a 1 if the clause _C<sub>i</sub>_ is satisfied by _s_ and 0 else. The cost vector _c_ contains then the weight each clause. In both Flip and Polm, the value of a solution is just a bit string, interpreted as a binary number. Therefore, we have that \(s'\) is the bit string and _c<sub>i</sub>_=2_<sup>i</sup>_. We say they use a _lexicographic cost function_. This motivates the following problem:

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Search Problem 2** (LocalLexMax-_k_-SAT)**.** LocalLexMax-_k_-SAT _is_ LocalMax- _k_-SAT _where the clause C<sub>i</sub> has a weight of_ 2_<sup>i</sup>. Equivalently, we can view the problem as a FLIP instance with n input bits and m output bits where every output bit is computed by a single k-clause._

We are now ready to state our first main result:

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 3.** LocalLexMax-4-SAT _is PLS-complete, and so is_ Flip _with depth-1 circuits._

We will prove Theorem 3 in Section 4. Note that LocalLexMax-2-SAT can be solved polynomially; in fact, we can even compute a global maximum by the following greedy algorithm:

1. Set _G<sub>m</sub>_:=1, the empty CNF, always true. 2. For _i=m_-1_,...,_0: set \(G_i:=G_{i+1}\wedge Ci\) if this is satisfiable; otherwise, set _G<sub>i</sub>_:=_G_<sub>_i_+1</sub>. This algorithm works for all _k_-CNF formulas as long as the clause weights are lexicographic; it is efficient as long as we can check efficiently whether \(G_{i+1}\wedge Ci\) is satisfiable. Similarly, LocalMaxCut with lexicographic costs is in P.

One of the main ways to show the PLS-hardness of a problem _L_ is a reduction from FLIP using Krentel’s technique[15, 16] of simulating multiple circuits, one on the current input and some on (a subset of) its neighborhood and using a gadget to switch to the best neighbor. One must then use the machinery of _L_ to simulate how the circuits evaluate their inputs and how one switches from the current solution to a better neighbor. This is used in the proof of Theorem 3 as well as in [20, 6, 7, 19, 21, 8]. These proofs are often quite long and complicated.

LocalLexMax-4-SAT is a special case of Flip that is still PLS-complete and combines the simple cost function of Flip with the simple combinatorial structure of CNF formulas. We argue that for reductions showing PLS-completeness, LocalLexMax-4-SAT can often be a better starting point than Flip, leading to simpler proofs and stronger results. We demonstrate this in two cases:

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 4.** Permutation Orbit Local Minimum _is PLS-complete even when restricted to permutations_ \(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_k\) _that generate an Abelian group._

We prove Theorem 4 in Section 3; in fact, we prove that it stays PLS-complete even if we require that all permutations in \(\langle\pi_1,\dots,\pi_k\rangle\) have order 2. In Section C we prove that it stays PLS-complete even if we require the group \(\langle\pi_1,\dots,\pi_k\rangle\) to be cyclic. This answers an open question and strengthens the result from [20] as Abelian and cyclic groups allow less freedom for the permutations and also admit a potentially faster brute-force algorithm as \(\pi\circ\sigma=\sigma\circ\pi\).

Our final application of Theorem 3 comes from algorithmic game theory:

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 5.** _Finding an_ \(\alpha\)_-equilibrium for_ \(\alpha>1\) _in a congestion game is PLS-complete when all delay functions are step functions or all are exponential functions or all are polynomials with positive coefficients._

Skopalik and Vöcking have shown that finding an \(\alpha\)-equilibrium in congestion games with step functions is PLS-complete[21]. Using Theorem 3, we can give a very short and simple proof of this fact. In the appendix of the work of Caragiannis, Fanelli, Gravin and Skopalik [3] this was also shown for polynomials with positive coefficients. Nonetheless, the question of the complexity of finding approximate Nash equilibria with positive coefficient polynomials was raised in [8, 22, 23].

Using LocalLexMax-4-SAT we get an extremely simple reduction for both cases that is also very regular and easy to analyze. In the light of this hardness result it is natural to ask whether there are useful parameters of the game that allow us to solve the problem efficiently when these parameters are small.

In all reductions the maximum number of players per resource is bounded (3 in [21], 2 in [3] and 4 in our work). Another interesting parameter is the maximum number of strategies per player. In [3, 21] this grows linearly with the input due to the \(\check{\mathrm{ck}}_{i,b}^j\) strategies of the _Y<sub>j</sub>_ players. Our reduction shows that the problem is hard even when each player has only two strategies.<sup>1</sup> We will prove Theorem 5 in Section 2.

All reductions in this work are tight, i.e. the standard algorithm that starts from a solution and moves to a better neighbor takes for any problem in the worst-case exponentially many steps and deciding if a solution is the result of the standard algorithm is PSPACE-complete. (see Section D).

## 2 Computing approximate Nash equilibria in congestion games - proof of Theorem 5

In a congestion game, there is a set _N_={1_,...,n_} of players and a set _E_ of resources. Each player \(i\in N\) has a set of \(strategiesS_i\subseteq 2^E\). Each resource \(e\in E\) has a \(delayde:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}\). A _strategy profile_ is a vector **s**=(_s_<sub>1</sub>_,s_<sub>2</sub>_,...,s<sub>n</sub>_) with \(si_i\in S_i\). The _load_ of a resource _e_ under profile **s** is the number of players using it: \(l(e,\mathbf{s}):=|\{i\in N|e\in si_i\}|\). This load causes a delay of _de(l(e,_**s**)). The cost of such a strategy profile **s** for a player _i_ is the sum of the delays of each resource they use, i.e. \(C_i(\mathbf{s})=\sum_{e\in s_i}d_e(l(e,\mathbf{s}))\). Players act selfishly and switch their strategy if it reduces the cost. A pure Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile **s**=(_s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>n</sub>_) where no player has an incentive to unilaterally change their strategy, i.e., if

\(\forall i\in N\forall s'_i\in S_i:C_i(\mathbf{s})\le C_i(s_1,\dots,s_{i-1},s'_i,s_{i+1},\dots,s_n).\)

For such games, a pure Nash equilibrium always exists, as shown by Rosenthal [18]. Fabrikant, Papadimitriou, Talwar [7] show that finding a pure Nash equilibrium is PLS-complete by giving a simple reduction from local NAE-3-SAT. When we assume that the players are lazy and only change their strategy if their cost decreases by a significant amount, we get the concept of an _approximate_ pure Nash equilibrium. More formally, for a real \(\alpha\ge 1\), an \(\alpha\)-equilibrium is a strategy profile **s**=(_s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>n</sub>_) such that

\(\forall i\in N\forall s'\in S_i:C_i(\mathbf{s})\le\alpha\cdot C_i(s_1,\dots,s_{i-1},s'_i,s_{i+1},\dots,s_n).\)

Skopalik and Vöcking [21] show that this is PLS-complete for any computable \(\alpha>1\) using an involved reduction from Flip and even more extended in [3] for polynomials with positive coefficients.

<sup>1</sup> Players with one strategy can be removed by changing the payoff functions, so this is the minimum number of strategies players can have in any (non-trivial) game.

It is not possible to reuse the general reduction from 3-SAT to show hardness of approximation. Consider the clauses \(A=\neg y\), _C=x_, \(C'=\neg x\) and \(D=x\vee y\) with the weights _w(A_)=8 , \(w(C)=w(C')=2\) and _w(D_)=1. The assignment \(x,y\mapsto 0,0\) has a weight of _w(C_)+_w(D_)=3, whereas flipping the value of x leads to an assignment of weight \(w'(C)=2\). Thus, this is an improving move, but not if it should improve by an \(\alpha\ge 2\) and similar examples exist for larger \(\alpha\). These problems don’t occur with lexicographic weights, and using a reduction from LocalLexMax-4-SAT, we can give a very short proof. \(\blacktriangleright\) **Proposition 6** (Skopalik and Vöcking [21])**.** _For any computable_ \(\alpha>1\) _and any congestion game G, finding an_ \(\alpha\)_-equilibrium is PLS-complete._ **Proof.** We reduce from LocalLexMax-4-SAT. Let \(F=C_0\wedge C_1\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{m-1}\) be a weighted 4- CNF formula with _w(Cj_)=2_j_. For an assignment \(\alpha\), define \(C(\alpha):=(C_{m-1}(\alpha),\dots,C_0(\alpha))\in\{0,1\}^m\). The total weight of satisfied clauses is thus simply \(C(\alpha)\), interpreted as a binary number. Thus, \(\mathrm{Value}(\alpha)\le\mathrm{Value}(\beta)\) if and only if \(C(\alpha)\unknown_\mathrm{lex}C(\beta)\), i.e., only the first differing bit matters. This means we can change the clause weights from 2_j_ to _cj_ for any \(c\ge 2\) and all the answers to \(\mathrm{Value}(\alpha)\le^?\mathrm{Value}(\beta)\) will stay the same. We choose \(c=\alpha+1\). A solution to LocalLexMax-4-SAT is an assignment that locally maximizes the weight of satisfied clauses. In the following proof it might be better to think about _minimizing_ the weight of _unsatisfied_ clauses (which is of course the same). We will now define the congestion game. The resources are the clauses _C_0_,...,C__m_-1. The players are the variables {_x_1_,...,xn_}. Player _xi_ has two strategies: \(\mathrm{true}_i:=\{C\in F|\neg x\in C\}\)
\(\mathrm{false}_i:=\{C\in F|x\in C\}.\) Note that strategy profiles in the game are in a 1-to-1 correspondence with the Boolean assignments to the variables of _F_. A player (i.e., variable _x_) uses the resources (i.e., clauses) that are _not_ satisfied by the current assignment and contain the variable _x_. The delay _dC_ of clause/resource _Cj_ is defined to be 0 if strictly fewer than _k_ players use it (where \(k\le 4\) is the size of _Cj_), and \(w(C_j)=(1+\alpha)^j\) if _k_ players do (note that _Cj_ can never be used by more than _k_ players). The more valuable clauses thus cause a higher delay for the player then less valuable clauses. Apart from the value \(1+\alpha\), this is roughly as in [7]. We must now show that a pure \(\alpha\)-Nash equilibrium corresponds to a local minimum of LocalLexMax-4-SAT. Contrapositively, we show that a variable flip that improves the weight of satisfied clauses corresponds to a player who will change their strategy. Consider an improving flip of variable _xi_ (from False to True, without loss of generality). There is an index _j_ such that _Cj_ used to be unsatisfied before the flip and is now satisfied, and the clauses _C__j_+1_,...,Cm_ do not change their status. The delay for player _xi_ before the flip is therefore at least \((1+\alpha)^j.\) (2.1) Since the flip does not change the status of _C__j_+1_,...,Cm_, the unsatisfied among them contain neither _x_ nor \(\bar{x}\) and thus do not contribute to the delay for player _x_. Thus, their delay after the flip is at most \(\sum_{l\le j-1}(1+\alpha)^l=\frac{(1+\alpha)^j-1}{\alpha}.\) (2.2) Thus, changing the strategy reduces the delay of player _xi_ at least by a factor of \(\alpha\), so this is not an \(\alpha\)-Nash equilibrium. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

In fact, we can replace the step functions with continuous functions. For this, we add dummy players with only one strategy consisting of occupying a single resource, so that any resource can be occupied by 4 players (effectively this corresponds to making all clauses have length exactly 4). We define a common function _f(x_) and set the delay of the resource _C<sub>j</sub>_ under load \(x\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}\) to _d<sub>C<sub>j</sub></sub>(x_)=_f(mx+j_). Note that _j\<m_, since _m_ is the number of clauses. We choose _f_ such that

\(f(x+1)\ge(1+\alpha)f(x)\) (2.3)

and \(f(x)\ge 0\) hold for any \(x\in[0,5m-1]\). The term in (2.1) is then _f(x_) for some _x\<_5_m_ and the term in Equation (2.2) is then \(\sum_{k<x}f(k)\) as flipping _x<sub>i</sub>_ may lead to all smaller clauses being false (that means 4 players using the clause resource) and in higher-priority clauses that contain _x<sub>i</sub>_, the number of unsatisfied literals may increase to some \(l\le 3\). This is a gross overestimate. From (2.3) it follows that \(f(k-i)\le(1+\alpha)^{-i}f(x)\) and thus (2.2) is at most

\(\sum_{k<x}f(k)=\sum_{i=1}^xf(x-i)\le f(x)\sum_{i=1}^x(1+\alpha)^{-i}\le f(x)\sum_{i=1}^\infty(1+\alpha)^{-i}=\frac{f(x)}{\alpha}.\)

Therefore this is an \(\alpha\)-improving move. Now setting \(f(x):=(1+\alpha)^x\) obviously fulfills (2.3); so does _f(x_):=_x<sup>d</sup>_ with \(d\ge 5mln(\alpha+1)\) since \((\frac{x+1}{x})^d\ge e^\frac{d}{x+1}\ge e^{d/5m}\ge\alpha+1\).

## 3 Permutation Orbit Local Minimum with Abelian groups - Proof of Theorem 4

We will show a PLS-reduction from LocalLexMax-4-SAT to Permutation Orbit Local Minimum where all the \(\pi_i\) commute. We use a technique by Buchheim and Jünger [2]. Let the 4-CNF \(F=C_1\wedge\cdots\wedge C_m\) be the input instance and _V_={_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_} its variables. Clause _C<sub>i</sub>_ has weight 2<sup>_m-i_</sup>. We assume for simplicity that each clause in _F_ has exactly four literals; the reduction for the general case is almost identical, but notation would become less readable. We will now describe the instance of Polm - set of positions, initial bit string, the commuting permutations, and, finally, the order on the positions.

**1. The set of positions.** For each 4-clause _C_ and each \(b\in\{0,1\}^4\) we construct a position _C<sub>b</sub>_. There is exactly one assignment \(b^*\in\{0,1\}^4\) to the four variables in _C_ that violates it; the corresponding position _C_<sub>_b_<sup>∗</sup></sub> is called a _violating position_ and denoted by _C_<sup>∗</sup>. We have a total of 16_m_ positions; among those, _m_ are violating.

**2. The initial bit string.** Our initial bit string \(\vec{s}\) puts a 1 on \(C_\vec{0}\) for each clause and a 0 on all other _C<sub>b</sub>_. This corresponds to the assignment that sets all variables to 0.

**3. The permutations.** For a variable _x_ and a clause _C_, let \(\pi_{x,C}\) be the permutation defined as follows:

**a.** If _x_ does not show up in _C_, then \(\pi_{x,C}\) is the identity.

**b.** If _x_ is the _i_-th variable of _C_ (with \(1\le i\le 4\)), then \(\pi_{x,C}\) is the involution that swaps each position _C<sub>b</sub>_ with position \(C_{b\oplus e_i}\).

So \(\pi_{x,C}\) basically switches the value of _x in clause C_. We define \(\pi_x\) to be

\(\pi_x:=\prod_{C\in F}\pi_{x,C}\)

so \(\pi_x\) switches the value of _x_ in every clause. Our set of generators is

\(G:=\{\pi_x|x\in V\}\)

**4. The ordering of the positions.** First come all the violating positions \(C_1^*,C_2^*,\dots,C_m^*\), using the same priority order as the clauses (with _C_<sub>1</sub> having the highest priority). Then come the 15_m_ non-violating positions, in some arbitrary order.

Consider a string \(\vec{v}\) in the orbit, meaning \(\vec{v}=\vec{s}\circ\sigma\) for some \(\sigma\in\langle G\rangle\). Then for each clause _C_, exactly one of the sixteen positions _C<sub>b</sub>_ has a 1 in \(\vec{v}\); this corresponds to some truth assignment to the variables in _C_. Those assignments agree globally and define an assignment \(\alpha_v:V\rightarrow\{0,1\}\).

**Proposition 7.** _Let_ \(1\le j\le m\) _and let_ \(\vec{v}\) _be in the orbit. Then v<sub>j</sub> is_ 1 _if and only if the corresponding assignment_ \(\alpha_v\) _violates C<sub>j</sub>._

Thus, if \(\alpha_v\) can be improved by flipping some variable _x_, then \(\vec{v}\circ\pi_x\) decreases the string lexicographically; Thus, a locally minimal string in the orbit corresponds to an assignment that cannot be improved by 1-flips i.e., a local optimum for LocalLexMax-4-SAT. This concludes the proof of Theorem 4.

## 4 Max 4-SAT with lexicographic costs - proof of Theorem 3

This is the main technical contribution of the paper. We will proceed in three steps.

**1.** In Section 4.1, we present a proof by Krentel[15, 16] that LocalMax-4-SAT is PLS- complete; we will make sure that the clause weights are "almost lexicographic", meaning that each clause weight is a power of two, and each weight appears for at most two clauses.

**2.** In Section 4.2 we modify this construction to achieve fully lexicographic weights; this requires a new idea and comes at the cost that we need to allow "double flips" for PLS-completeness, that is, the neighborhood relation is defined by flipping up to two variables.

**3.** In Section 4.3 we show how to simulate double flips by a sequence of single flips. This will then prove Theorem 3.

## 4.1 Krentel’s Construction: Reducing Flip to LocalMax-4-SAT With Almost Lexicographic Clause Weights

Let \(C'\) be an instance of Flip: a Boolean circuit with _n_ inputs and _m_ outputs. We can transform this into a new circuit _C_ with _n_ inputs and _m+n_ outputs that also computes the best neighbor of the current input. We can assume without loss of generality that _C_ uses only NAND-gates. We create two copies of _C_, called TOP and BOTTOM. For every input \(1\le i\le n\) of _C_ we create two variables \(x_i^T\) and \(x_i^B\), giving a total of 2_n_ input variables. For every gate _j_ of _C_ we create variables \(g_j^T\) and \(g_j^B\). Of those, 2(_m+n_) correspond to the outputs of TOP and BOTTOM. It is advantageous to give them synonyms: we denote the _m+n_ output variables of TOP \(v_1^T,\dots,v_m^T,z_1^T,\dots,z_n^T\) and those of BOTTOM \(v_1^B,\dots,v_m^B,z_1^B,\dots,z_n^B\). Altogether, if \(C'\) has _s_ NAND-gates, we get 2_s_ gate variables, thus a total of 2(_n+s_) variables.

**Feeding output back to the inputs.** The variables represent a partial evaluation of the two circuits. NAND-gates can temporarily be incorrect, for example if \(g_j^T\) is a gate variable with inputs \(y_1^T\) and \(y_2^T\) (those being either gate variables or input variables), but all three variables are set to 1, because the correct output of the gate would be 0. Also, we connect the last _n_ output bits (the "successor output") of TOP to the input of BOTTOM and vice versa. The intuition is that we can (1) flip gate variables in TOP to make every gate

in TOP correct; (2) flip input variables in BOTTOM to make them agree with TOP’s output; (3) flip gate variables in BOTTOM to make all gates there correct; (4) flip input variables in TOP to make them agree with BOTTOM’s output. By that time most likely some gates of TOP will be incorrect again (by us having meddled with its input variables) and so we go back to step (1) and repeat. By creating the right clauses and choosing appropriate weights we can make sure that each flip increases the weight of the satisfied clauses as long as the value outputs of the circuits increase.

**The active and the inactive circuit.** To make this idea work, we need an additional variable _f_, the flip variable, which indicates which circuit we consider to be _active_: TOP (if _f_=1) or BOTTOM (if _f_=0). The idea is now that gates in the active circuit should be correctly evaluated at all times and that _f_ should be flipped only when both circuits are correctly evaluated and the currently inactive circuit has better output than the other: if \((v_1^A\dots v_m^A)>_\mathrm{lex}(v_1^I\dots,v_m^I)\) where \(A\in\{\mathrm{T},\mathrm{B}\}\) denotes the active circuit and _I_ the inactive circuit. See Figure 1 for an illustration.

**The clauses.** We will now describe in detail the clauses of our 4-CNF formula _F_. They come in groups, which we list from most-important to least-important.

**1. Every gate in the active circuit should be correct.** When a gate _g<sub>j</sub>_ has inputs _y_<sub>1</sub> and _y_<sub>2</sub>, we write

\(f\rightarrow(g_j^T\leftrightarrow\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^T,y_2^T))\) (4.1)

and express this as a conjunction of four 4-clauses. Similarly, for the case that BOTTOM is active:

\(\neg f\rightarrow(g_j^B\leftrightarrow\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^B,y_2^B))\) (4.2)

Within this group, the ordering of the clauses follow the topological ordering of the gates (when _g_ feeds into _h_, then _g_ comes before _h_ and the clauses thusly produced come first, too. Within the eight clauses of (4.1-4.2) for a single gate, the order is arbitrary.

**2. The value output of the active circuit should be large.** For each value output position \(1\le i\le m\) we create two 2-clauses: \((f\rightarrow v_i^T)\) and \((\neg f\rightarrow v_i^B)\). The clauses are ordered from _i_=1 (most important) to _i=m_ (least important), and for the same _i_, the two clauses have equal weight (here we lose perfect lexicographicality).

**3. Successor output of active circuit should be input of inactive circuit.** We write this as

\(f\rightarrow(z_j^T=x_j^B)\text{and}\neg f\rightarrow(z_j^B=x_j^T).\) (4.3)

The ordering within this group is arbitrary.

**4. All gates should be correctly evaluated,** whether in the active or inactive circuit.

\(g_j^T\leftrightarrow\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^T,y_2^T)\text{and}g_j^B\leftrightarrow\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^B,y_2^B)\) (4.4)

We call clauses in Group 1 _hard clauses_ because they would always stay satisfied on an improving path, and if violated can be easily corrected. It is straightforward to check that in a local optimum of this LocalMax-4-SAT-instance, all gates are evaluated correctly and the output of the active circuit agrees with the input of the inactive. Thus, it holds that (**v**_<sup>A</sup>,_**z**_<sup>A</sup>_)=_C_(**x**_<sup>A</sup>_) and (**v**_<sup>I</sup>,_**z**_<sup>I</sup>_)=_C_(**x**_<sup>I</sup>_)=_C_(**z**_<sup>A</sup>_). If **v**_<sup>I</sup>\><sub>lex</sub>_** **v**_<sup>A</sup>_, then flipping the value of _f_ would (i) keep clauses in Group 1 satisfied; (ii) improve the weight of satisfied clauses in Group 2, and (iii) possibly violate clauses in Group 3. By the chosen weights, this would be an improving flip. Thus, if we have a local optimum of this LocalMax-4-SAT-instance, then \(\mathbf{v}^I\le_{lex}\mathbf{v}^A\) and **x**_<sup>A</sup>_ is indeed a solution of the original Flip instance.

## 4.2 Making Weights Fully Lexicographic By Allowing Double Flips

The trouble lies in Group 2. If we naively decree that \((f\rightarrow v_i^T)\) be more valuable than (actually, twice as) \((\neg f\rightarrow v_i^B)\), then the reduction would become incorrect: if **v**_<sup>T</sup>_=(01_..._) and **v**_<sup>B</sup>_=(00_..._) and BOTTOM is active, then flipping _f_ from 0 to 1 would improve the output but violate \((f\rightarrow v_i^T)\) instead of \((\neg f\rightarrow v_i^B)\), thus reducing the weight of satisfied clauses. We are stuck in a local optimum that does not correspond to a local optimum of Flip.

To solve this problem, we create a _global output register_ **o** consisting of _m_ variables _o_<sub>1</sub>_,...,o<sub>m</sub>_. The idea is now that (1) **o** should be large, but (2) not larger than the active output. When switching active and inactive circuits, we can flip _f and simultaneously_ the improving position of **o**, improving (1) but temporarily violating (2). To make this work we need to choose the order of the clauses in Group 2 carefully.

**2. The global output register should be large, but not larger than the active output.** For each \(1\le i\le m\), we replace the two old clauses \((f\rightarrow v_i^T)\) and \((\neg f\rightarrow v_i^B)\) by

\(\text{the}i^\mathrm{th}\text{TOP control clause}C_i^T:=(f\rightarrow(o_i\le v_i^T))\) (4.5)

\(\text{the}i^\mathrm{th}\text{BOTTOM control clause}C_i^B:=(\neg f\rightarrow(o_i\le v_i^B))\) (4.6)

\(\text{the}i^\mathrm{th}\text{output clause}C_i^O:=(o_i)\) (4.7)

The _m_ blocks are ordered from 1 (most important) to _m_ (least important) and within each block, the three clauses<sup>2</sup> are ordered as shown above.

Now if we have a local optimum of this LocalLexMax-4-SAT instance, then by the same reasoning as in Section 4.1, all circuits are correctly evaluated and BOTTOM’s input is TOP’s output and thus (**v**_<sup>A</sup>,_**z**_<sup>A</sup>_)=_C_(**x**_<sup>A</sup>_) and (**v**_<sup>I</sup>,_**z**_<sup>I</sup>_)=_C_(**x**_<sup>I</sup>_)=_C_(**z**_<sup>A</sup>_). Additionally, it holds that **o**=**v**_<sup>A</sup>_. If \(\mathbf{v}^I\le_{lex}\mathbf{v}^A\) we have found a solution to the original Flip instance. Otherwise, **v**_<sup>I</sup>\><sub>lex</sub>_**v**_<sup>A</sup>_=**o**. Let _i_ be the first position where they differ, so \(v_i^I=1\) and \(v_i^A=0\) (and thus _o<sub>i</sub>_=0). Now flipping the value _f_ and simultaneously setting _o<sup>i</sup>_ to 1 keeps Group 1 satisfied; the clauses in blocks \(1,\cdots\le i-1\) of Group 2 do not change; in block _i_ we gain (_o<sub>i</sub>_) and now satisfy all three clauses; we might wreak havoc in blocks _i_+1_,...,m_ and Group 3, but gaining (_o<sub>i</sub>_) outweighs all this. Thus, if we are not at a local optimum for Flip, we aren’t at one for LocalLexMax-4-SAT, either, and the reduction is correct.

## 4.3 Replacing double flips with single flips

In the previous section, we need to flip two variables to simulate a flip in the circuit instance. Flipping only _o<sub>i</sub>_ from 0 to 1 will violate the _i_<sup>th</sup> control clause of the active circuit, and flipping _f_ alone does not increase and likely reduces the payoff. We introduce new variables that we call _shadow variables_, denoted by \(s_i^B\) and \(s_i^T\) for every output bit. Their purpose is to temporarily fulfill a control clause so that we can flip _o<sub>i</sub>_. Then we can flip _f_ and continue as above.

We need to introduce two new groups of hard clauses, 0 and 1b, the latter located between group 1 and 2; modify group 2; and add groups 5 and 6. Groups 1, 3, and 4 are as above.

**0. Both inputs are equal or neighbors of the flip instance.** These hard clauses prevent assignments where the inputs of both circuits have a Hamming distance greater than one. They are not strictly needed for PLS-completeness but ensure _tightness_ of the reduction (see Section D).

\(\forall i\neq j:x_i^T\neq x_i^B\rightarrow x_j^T=x_j^B\) (4.8)

The ordering among Group 0 clauses is arbitrary.

**1b. Proper use of shadow variables.** These hard clauses have the purpose to disallow using shadow variables if there is no flip to be done. All clauses in this group can be satisfied by setting a shadow variable to false.

Shadow variables should be turned on only when the corresponding circuit is correctly evaluated and, in case it is the inactive circuit, it is reading its correct input, namely the best-neighbor output of the active circuit. Thus, for every output position \(1\le i\le m\) and every input position \(1\le j\le n\) we produce

\((s_i^B\wedge f)\rightarrow(z_j^T=x_j^B)\text{and}(s_i^T\wedge\neg f)\rightarrow(z_j^B=x_j^T)\) (4.9)

saying that a "shadowed inactive" circuit must read the correct input. Second, we require a shadowed circuit to be correct in all gates. Thus, if a gate _g<sub>j</sub>_ has inputs _y_<sub>1</sub> and _y_<sub>2</sub>, we produce

\(s_i^T\rightarrow(g_j^T\leftrightarrow\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^T,y_2^T))\text{and}s_i^B\rightarrow(g_j^B\leftrightarrow\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^B,y_2^B))\) (4.10)

<sup>2</sup> \(C_i^T\) and \(C_i^B\) are indeed clauses: \((\neg f\vee\neg o_i\vee v_i^T)\) and \((f\vee\neg o_i\vee v_i^B)\).

Lastly, shadow variables must not be used in vain--meaning they should be used only when they indicate a position where the inactive output is better than the active one. Why is this necessary? When _i_ is the most significant bit in which the active output is 0 but the inactive is 1 (so _i_ is where we can improve things), we can be sure that all shadow variables of the positions 1_,...,i_-1 are off, which will be important later. \(s_i^B\rightarrow v_i^B\text{and}s_i^B\rightarrow\neg v_i^T\) (4.11) \(s_i^T\rightarrow v_i^T\text{and}s_i^T\rightarrow\neg v_i^B\) (4.12) The order among the clauses in this group is arbitrary. All clauses so far (correctness clauses and proper use clauses) stay fulfilled along the canonical path and are never violated when only doing improving steps. If violated, we can always satisfy them by correcting the input of the inactive circuit (group 0), correcting the output of gates (group 1), or by deactivating shadow variables (group 1b). **2. The global output register should be large, but not larger than the active output.**
The first three clauses are almost exactly the same as in the previous section, except that control clauses can also be fulfilled by the shadow variables of the other circuit. The last clauses are used to switch the active circuit after the global output was improved via a shadow variable. \(C_i^T:=f\rightarrow(o_i\le v_i^T)\vee s_i^B\) (4.13) \(C_i^B:=\neg f\rightarrow(o_i\le v_i^B)\vee s_i^T\) (4.14) \(C_i^O:=o_i\) (4.15) \((o_i\wedge s_i^B)\rightarrow\neg f\) (4.16) \((o_i\wedge s_i^T)\rightarrow f\) (4.17) **5. Use shadow variables at improvable positions.** If the inactive circuit is better at a position _i_ than the active circuit, these clauses will be false unless the shadow variable is turned on. Shadow variables of the active circuit have, however, no incentive to be switched on from here. The order is arbitrary in this group. \((f\wedge v_i^B\wedge\neg v_i^T)\rightarrow s_i^B\text{and}(\neg f\wedge v_i^T\wedge\neg v_i^B)\rightarrow s_i^T\) (4.18) **6. Turn off shadow variables**
The final set of clauses allows deactivating any shadow variable. The order is arbitrary in this group. \(\neg s_i^B\text{and}\neg s_i^T\) (4.19) Previously, we flipped both _f_ and a global output _oi_ in order to gain an improvement. The new idea is to first set the shadow variable \(s_i^B\) to 1 (without loss of generality BOTTOM is inactive), for which clause (4.18) gives us an incentive. Now the control clause \(f\rightarrow(o_i\le v_i^T)\vee s_i^B\) (4.13) is additionally satisfied by \(s_i^B\), which enables us to flip the global output _oi_ to 1; finally this leads to flipping _f_. As a last step we can turn all shadow variables off again in the now active circuit BOTTOM using group 6. PLS-completeness now follows from the following lemma, which we prove in Section A: \(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 8.** _Let_ \(\alpha\) _be a locally optimal assignment to the 4-CNF just constructed and consider_ **x**_A, the input variables of the active circuit. Then_ \(\alpha(\mathbf{x}^A)\) _is a local optimum of the_ Flip _instance C._

## 5 Conclusion and open problems

We added two members to the club of PLS-complete problems with lexicographic costs: LocalLexMax-4-SAT and Abelian Polm. We believe that as a point for further reductions, LocalLexMax-4-SAT is better than Flip due to its simple structure while preserving the lexicographical costs. We demonstrated this by showing that finding approximate Nash equilibria is PLS-complete, and the simple structure of lexicographic costs allowed us to use nice continuous delay functions. Additionally, all reductions in this work are tight (see Section D).

Multiple open problems remain: While LocalLexMax-_k_-SAT is PLS-complete for _k_=4 and in P for _k_=2, the case _k_=3 is open. Our reduction cannot easily be changed to produce 3-clauses: we already need 3-clauses to model the correct evaluation of a circuit (2-clauses don’t suffice because 2-SAT is in NL and circuit evaluation is P-complete); and then we need an additional variable _f_ to temporarily de-activate one copy of the circuit. It is also open whether LocalMax-4-SAT stays PLS-complete if every variable appears a bounded number of times.

Secondly, in our reduction and the reduction in [20] for Polm the number of permutations grows with the input size. What happens if we only have a fixed number of permutations _k_? For _k_=1 this is in P [14, 20] but even for _k_=2 it is open.

Thirdly, what happens if the delay functions in the congestion game are polynomials of bounded degree _d_ (and perhaps weighted)? While upper bounds are known, there are no lower bounds known for those \(\alpha\) where the problem is in PLS[4, 5, 11]. In [5] it is shown that for \(\alpha\in\mathcal{O}(\frac{d}{lnd})\) deciding the existence of an approximate Nash-equilibrium is NP-hard if the game is weighted. LocalLexMax-4-SAT might be a helpful intermediate problem to reach this target.

Lastly, another interesting PLS problem with lexicographic costs might be the traveling salesman problem as here it is also not feasible to check if there exists a solution using a set of edges. Known reductions[12, 19] start however from Max-Cut and are therefore not adaptable for lexicographic costs.

## A Remaining proofs for Max-4-SAT

In this section, we give the remaining proofs for Section 4.3. The reduction given above transforms a circuit _C_ (an instance of Flip) into a 4-CNF-formula _F=F(C_) (an instance of LocalMax-4-SAT). One step was to augment the circuit _C_ to not only output the _m_-bit vector representing the _value_ of its input **x**, but also the best neighbor of **x**. We denote by \(C_V(\mathbf{x})\in\{0,1\}^m\) the value and by _C<sub>N</sub>_(**x**) the best neighbor. Let \(\alpha\) be a truth assignment to the variables of _F_ and _f_ the _flip variable_. Recall that we call the TOP circuit _active_ if \(\alpha(f)=1\); we call BOTTOM active if \(\alpha(f)=0\). We call the other circuit _inactive_. We define a function _g_ that maps assignments \(\alpha\) of _F_ to circuits input for _C_ as follows:

\(g(\alpha)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\alpha(x^B) & ,\text{if}\alpha(f)=0 \\
\alpha(x^T) & ,\text{if}\alpha(f)=1
\end{array}\right.\)

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 9.** _Let_ \(\alpha\) _be a locally optimal assignment to the variables of F. Then_ \(g(\alpha)\) _is a solution to the flip instance C._

**Proof.** We will assume without loss of generality that \(\alpha(f)=1\), i.e., the TOP circuit is active.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 10.** \(\alpha\) _maps all shadow variables of the active circuit TOP to_ 0.

**Proof.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that \(\alpha(s_i^T)=1\) for some \(1\le i\le m\). What happens when we change \(\alpha(s_i^T)\) to 0? Clause groups 0, 1, 3 and 4 do not contain shadow variables. Clauses of groups 1b and 6 contain only the negative literal \(\neg s_i^T\), so the change can only improve. In group 2, \(s_i^T\) occurs in \(C_i^B:=\neg f\rightarrow(o_i\le v_i^B)\vee s_i^T\) (4.14) and \((o_i\wedge s_i^T)\rightarrow f\) (4.17), and in group 5 only in \((\neg f\wedge v_i^T\wedge\neg v_i^B)\rightarrow s_i^T\) (4.18). All three clauses are and stay satisfied by \(\alpha(f)=1\). Group 6 contains \((\neg s_i^T)\) (4.19), so the satisfied weight improves, meaning that \(\alpha\) was no local optimum. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 11.** _In_ \(\alpha\)_, all gate variables in the active circuit are correct, i.e. their output matches what an actual_ NAND _would do for the current values of the inputs._

**Proof.** Suppose not, so there is a gate variable \(g_j^T\neq\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^T,y_2^T)\), where \(y_1^T,y_2^T\) are the variables feeding into gate _g<sub>j</sub>_ (either earlier gates or input variables). Changing the value of \(g_j^T\) leaves clauses in group 0 unaffected; in group 1 we satisfy an additional clause of \(f\rightarrow(g_j^T\leftrightarrow\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^T,y_2^T))\) (4.1) belonging to gate _j_ in TOP while not violating any gate coming before _j_; we might violate lower-priority clauses. The total satisfied weight improves and \(\alpha\) was not a local optimum. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 12.** _Suppose_ \(\alpha(s_i^B)=1\) _for some shadow variable_ \(s_i^B\)_. Then all gate variables in_ BOTTOM _are correct._

**Proof.** Otherwise, if some gate variable \(g_j^B\) were incorrect, we could simply change \(\alpha(s_i^B)\) to 0; this would not affect groups 0 and 1; in group 1b the currently violated clause \(s_i^B\rightarrow(g_j^B\leftrightarrow\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^B,y_2^B)\) (4.10) would become satisfied, and no additional clause in group 1b would become violated, so this would improve the satisfied weight, and \(\alpha\) would not be a local optimum. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 13.** _In_ \(\alpha\)_, all gate variables in the inactive circuit are correct._

**Proof.** If some \(\alpha(s_i^B)=1\) this follows from Lemma 12. So we can assume (\*) that \(\alpha(s_i^B)=0\) for all shadow variables. For the sake of contradiction, suppose some gate variable \(g_j^B\) is incorrect: \(g_j^B\neq\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^B,y_2^B)\). What happens when we flip \(g_j^B\)? Clauses in group 0 are unaffected; clauses in group 1 concerning the bottom circuit are of the form \(\neg f\rightarrow(g_{j^\prime}^B\leftrightarrow\mathrm{NAND}(y_3^B,y_4^B))\) (4.2) and thus are and stay satisfied by \(\alpha(f)=1\). Group 1b stays satisfied because all shadow variables are 0 (in TOP by Lemma 10; in BOTTOM by assumption (\*)). If \(g_j^B\) is a value output variable \(v_i^B\) then group 2 contains \(\neg f\rightarrow(o_i\le v_i^B)\vee s_i^T\) (4.6); if \(g_j^B\) is a best-neighbor output variable \(z_{j^\prime}^B\) then group 3 contains clause \(\neg f\rightarrow(z_{j^\prime}^B=x_{j^\prime}^T)\) (4.3); both are and stay satisfied by \(\alpha(f)=1\). In group 4, changing the value of \(g_j^B\) will satisfy all of \(g_j^B\leftrightarrow\mathrm{NAND}(y_1^B,y_2^B)\), of which at least one was previously violated, and violate only lower-priority clauses, due to the clauses being ranked by the topological order on the gates. Because if there were, then this would not be an improving move in the LocalLexMax-4-SAT instance but might be in the newly created instances since it changes the delay on some more important resource from 3 to 2 while the delay on some less important resource increases from 1 to 2. Similarly, in the Polm instance this would mean that some very important fulfilling position by the order has a one and after applying it we map the one to some less important fulfilling position.

By Proposition 22 we know however that these internal improving flips can never occur and any flip changes the truth value of at least some clause. Thus, any improving flip in the f(I) instance here is an improving flip in the original instance _I_.

For cyclic Polm from the previous section the same proof idea works, but as R we choose the permutations that define an assignment, i.e. there are no ones at bad-color positions.

## E FP-completeness for LocalLexMax-2-SAT

In contrast to the decision variant 2-SAT, which is NL-complete, and the arbitrarily-weighted LocalMax-2-SAT, which is PLS-complete[19], we show that LocalMax-2-SAT with lexicographic costs (i.e. LocalLexMax-2-SAT) is FP-complete. We have already seen a polynomial time algorithm in the introduction; now we will show hardness.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Proposition 24.** LocalLexMax-2-SAT _is FP-hard._

**Proof.** We reduce from the circuit evaluation problem. We are given a circuit _C_ and an input \(\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^n\). The gates of _C_ are given in topological order. The goal is to compute \(C(\mathbf{x})\in\{0,1\}^m\), i.e., the output of the circuit. We can assume that the circuit consists only of NAND-gates. We use a variable _xi<sub>i</sub>_ for each input and a variable _g<sub>j</sub>_ for each gate.

The highest clauses fix the input variables to the current input. Afterwards, we use the following three clauses for each gate. If gate _g<sub>j</sub>_ has inputs _y_<sub>1</sub> and _y_<sub>2</sub>, we produce the following block containing three clauses:

1. \(\neg y_1\rightarrow g_j\)

2. \(\neg y_2\rightarrow g_j\)

3. \(\neg g_j\)

The blocks are ordered according to the topological ordering of the circuit; within each block they are ordered as shown above.

We claim that in any local optimum \(\alpha\), it holds that _g<sub>j</sub>_=NAND(_y_<sub>1</sub>_,y_<sub>2</sub>) holds. Suppose that this is not the case.

**Case 1:** \(\alpha(g_j)=1\) and \(\alpha(y_1)=\alpha(y_1)=1\). Then the third clause above, \(\neg g_j\), is violated, and setting _g<sub>j</sub>_ to 0 will satisfy all three clauses above.

**Case 0:** \(\alpha(g_j)=0\) and at least one of _y_<sub>1</sub>_,y_<sub>2</sub> is mapped to 0. Then one of the first two clauses must is violated; flipping _g_ satisfies it; it will violate the third clause, but it is still an improving flip.

So we conclude that under \(\alpha\) every gate is correctly evaluated. Therefore, the value of the _m_ output gate variables under \(\alpha\) give us the correct output of the circuit: _C_(**x**).
